summary:
On 4 July 2010, Popular Front of India (PFI) members attacked Malayalam professor T. J. Joseph in Kerala, severing his right hand. The assault followed a blasphemy controversy over an exam question; Joseph said its wording was adapted from a published work and meant no offence.

In March 2010, Joseph set a question asking students to punctuate a dialogue between God and a character named “Muhammed.” The passage came from a book by filmmaker P. T. Kunju Muhammed, who described a character based on a man with schizophrenia speaking to God. The name was intended to refer to the author but could be read as referring to the Prophet Muhammad. After a newspaper report prompted protests, police charged Joseph, and Newman College suspended him and apologised.

Eight attackers stopped Joseph’s vehicle near his home, chopped off his hand, stabbed his thigh, and attacked his sister and mother. He underwent a 16-hour operation. The family said it forgave the attackers. The university later called the question an unintentional error and revoked his suspension, but the college dismissed him in September, saying he had hurt religious sentiments. He was not reinstated; his wife died by suicide in 2014 amid the family’s financial and emotional strain.

Police described the assault as a planned operation and arrested or charged numerous PFI members and alleged associates. They seized weapons, explosives and other materials in raids. The National Investigation Agency initially said it would not investigate, and the state government told the High Court investigators had found no link between PFI and al-Qaeda, Lashkar-e-Taiba or Hizbul Mujahideen. A charge sheet against 27 PFI activists was filed in January 2011. One main accused, Savad, was arrested in January 2024 after 13 years on the run.

Kerala’s Assembly and Muslim, Christian and political groups condemned the attack; several Muslim organisations called it contrary to Islam and sought to isolate PFI. The college’s dismissal drew criticism from writers, teachers’ groups and cultural organisations. Media commentary condemned the assault as an attack on freedom of expression and warned of religious extremism. The state Home Minister also said authorities knew of a local Dar-ul Khada for civil disputes but had received no complaints of “Taliban-style” rulings.
unsupportedClaims: Political groups, apart from the Kerala State Assembly, condemned the attack.
